systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Vérification des sources complémentaires : avant de rédiger, vérifie que chaque SOURCE numérotée à partir de 2 traite bien du MÊME fait que la SOURCE 1 (même événement, mêmes acteurs). Ignore entièrement celles qui n'en traitent pas et donne leurs numéros dans « sources_ecartees ». Si, sans elles, la matière ne suffit pas pour un article fiable, réponds seulement {"insuffisant": true, "titre": "…", "texte": "…"} : une brève en français (titre de 90 caractères au plus, 2 à 3 phrases d'environ 450 caractères), uniquement d'après la SOURCE 1.
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Le texte réunit plusieurs sources sur le même sujet (SOURCE 1, SOURCE 2…). Croise-les sans rien ajouter ; si elles divergent, dis-le en nommant la source.
Source : WSJ
Rubrique : Sanctions et export
Date du flux : 17/11/2026
Titre d'origine : EU Sanctions Irish Journalist Over Russian Disinformation

ARTICLE :
SOURCE 1 (WSJ) :
EU Sanctions Irish Journalist Over Russian Disinformation WSJ

SOURCE 2 (RTE.ie) :
Irish journalist Chay Bowes has been sanctioned by the EU as an alleged propagandist for the Russian government.
The listing was announced by EU foreign ministers meeting in Brussels.
In a statement, member states said that Mr Bowes, who works for the Russian media outlet RT, had "participated in information manipulation and dissemination of narratives that legitimise and sustain the ongoing Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine."
He was one of 113 people and entities listed by EU foreign ministers in connection with Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Member states listed Russian television figures Vitaly Eliseev and Petr Marchenko, as well as Ukrainian-born blogger and military commentator Yurii Podoliaka alongside Mr Bowes.
Mr Bowes, who describes himself on his Instagram profile as an "Irish journalist, writer, broadcaster and troublemaker", is a former shareholder in, and founding member of, Irish news website The Ditch.
He was invited by Russia to address the UN Security Council by video link in 2023, when he blamed the war on NATO, describing a "frenzied, incalculable, loosely regulated" flood of weapons into Ukraine.
He was introduced at the UN as a "scholar specialising in small arms and munitions".
He said that NATO planners and an "ever-hawkish Anglosphere" were driving the "seemingly perpetual escalation of military aid to Ukraine".
His comments were condemned by Ukraine's ambassador to the UN at the time.
In a legal text, 45-year-old Mr Bowes is described as "an Irish citizen working as a correspondent for the Russian transnational influence channel RT International."
The text says he has been the host of an RT show called 'Moscow Mules' since February 2024 and that he co-founded a pro-Russian disinformation network called The Islander News.
It states: "Bowes is involved in numerous information operations conducted by the Foundation to Battle Injustice (R-FBI), which was created by the Wagner Group and listed by the [European] Union on July 2025."
The text says Bowes is also involved in "the regular amplification of content produced by the Russian Information Manipulation Set (IMS) Storm-1516."
The text concluded that Bowes was "implementing, supporting and facilitating actions or policies attributable to the Government of the Russian Federation which undermine or threaten democracy, the rule of law, stability or security in the Union, in an international organisation and in third countries, by planning, directing, engaging in, directly or indirectly, supporting or otherwise facilitating the use of coordinated information manipulation and interference."
Mr Bowes said in a social media post that "the authoritarian EU sanctioned me, no recourse to defend myself, no hearing, no evidence" and insisted that "Their allegations against me are utterly baseless".
He added: "They want to bully me into silence, they want to deny you your God-given right to hear dissenting opinions, they want to kill freedom of speech."
People Before Profit leader Richard Boyd Barrett, also writing on social media, called the sanction "A sinister move seriously threatening free speech and press".
"RT is a mouthpiece for Russian state that never criticises Putin but we have lots of voices on western media who push NATO, EU, US, Israeli propaganda with no sanction," he said.
The EU also listed 24 individuals connected to Russia’s Social Design Agency (SDA), a Moscow-based public relations company, which, according to a statement, "carries out large scale information manipulation and interference projects funded, directed and supervised by the Russian Presidential Administration."
Foreign ministers said the SDA "systematically manipulates the media and social media environment, spreads pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation and foreign information manipulation and interference campaigns".
The listings also include nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions.
Speaking on her arrival at a monthly EU foreign ministers meeting this morning, Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee said the listings came ahead of further discussions this week on a broader 22nd sanctions package on Russia.
Watch: Helen McEntee says EU has agreed on sanctions against 133 people, entities
Ukraine's financial, humanitarian needs assessed
EU foreign ministers are meeting to assess Ukraine's financial and humanitarian needs as Russia continues to destroy the country’s energy and water infrastructure.
The meeting comes in the wake of Friday’s informal EU summit in Dublin, at which EU leaders agreed the format for Europe’s involvement in potential peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, brokered by the United States.
Ministers will discuss ways of getting Ukraine the air defence systems it needs to counter Russia’s escalating waves of ballistic missile and jet-powered drone strikes.
Russia is continuing to strike Ukraine’s energy and water infrastructure, causing misery for millions of civilians, while also hitting the country’s grain exports in the Black Sea, a vital source of income.
Ministers will hear from their Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha on the country’s needs as winter tightens its grip.
On Wednesday, the European Commission will come forward with a proposal on how to tackle Ukraine’s €70 billion funding gap next year, while on Thursday the so-called Coalition of the Willing will meet in Berlin.
That is the ad hoc group of some 36 countries, led by the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, which could provide a peace keeping or peace enforcement mission in Ukraine should a ceasefire take effect.
Ms McEntee welcomed the prospect of Europe being present at negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, and the agreement in Dublin on Friday among EU leaders as to the structure of the European negotiating team.
She said: "I think naturally there will be a question as to how this works next. Importantly, it was agreed that Europe, firstly, would be around the table. That has not been the case until recently.
"It's really important now that we have a structure beyond that to make sure that any meetings that happen, that we have an agreed mandate, that we have an agreed position, that we focus on not just the security environment, because I think we tend to focus just on the security environment post a ceasefire.
"We need to look at politically where Europe needs to be involved. You need to look at economically where Europe needs to be involved from a humanitarian situation. What more we can do while also then focusing on the security aspect of it."
She added: "In the wake of all of this positive momentum, Russia has clearly not changed its position. It is continuing its attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure."

Ceasefire needed before peace talks, says Kallas
Earlier, EU foreign police chief Kaja Kallas said that Europe will need to see concessions from Russia and a ceasefire in Ukraine before serious peace talks could begin.
She also stressed the need for Europe to concentrate on the substance of any possible peace agreement and have a reply to Russia's "maximum demands".
France and Britain will hold a conference on 4 December on tackling Russia's "shadow fleet", France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.
"I will host in Paris on December 4, at the request of the President of the Republic, an international conference dedicated to the fight against the Russian shadow fleet," Mr Barrot told reporters at the meeting in Brussels.
Sanctions on Russia for invading Ukraine and aimed at cutting its oil revenue have spawned a fleet of often ageing and unregulated vessels helping Moscow keep its crude exports flowing.
EU naval forces last week boarded a suspected Russian shadow fleet crude tanker in the Mediterranean, Ms Kallas said yesterday.
Increasing danger of nuclear accident flagged
The risk of a nuclear accident in Ukraine is increasing this winter, nuclear safety regulators representing 38 countries has said, urging Russia to stop its attacks on the country's power infrastructure.
Moscow has stepped up its drone and missile attacks on Ukrainian energy installations, such as plants, power lines and electricity substations, a system already weakened after nearly five years of conflict.
"Together we... express our deep concern about the increasing risks to nuclear safety arising from Russia's war against Ukraine, and its continued attacks on the country's energy infrastructure," the bodies said in a joint statement seen by Reuters ahead of publication.
"Together, (we) see an urgent need for Russia to cease attacks against Ukraine's nuclear facilities and the energy infrastructure essential to their safe operation."
The regulators' key concern is that, without a stable electricity supply from the grid, it becomes more and more difficult for Ukrainian nuclear plants to keep their nuclear material cool and avoid a meltdown.
If that were to occur, there could be releases of radioactivity into the air as happened during the 1986 Chornobyl disaster, considered to be the world's worst civil nuclear accident.
Ukraine hits key Crimean bridge
Ukraine fired hundreds of drones at Russia overnight, aiming towards Moscow and hitting a symbolic bridge that links the annexed Crimean peninsula to Russia.
The strike on the bridge appeared to inflict only minor damage, though it drew an angry response from the Kremlin.
Ukraine launched 1,336 drones in the barrage, Moscow's defence ministry said in a statement, the second-highest daily figure so far this year, according to an AFP tally of official Russian statements.
The barrage came days before a summit in Shenzhen between President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. US officials say Russia's war against Ukraine is not expected to be a focus of the talks.
"The enemy has hit the Crimea bridge," Crimea's Russian-installed governor Sergey Aksyonov wrote on Telegram.
He did not say whether anyone was killed or wounded in the strike.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later told reporters that there was "minor damage" and that traffic was continuing.
He also issued a rare admission of vulnerability in Russia's air defence system.
"Unfortunately, no system in the world can provide 100 percent protection against such large-scale strikes on various targets," he said.
The bridge has been a key target for Ukraine since Russia launched its offensive in February 2022.
It has been struck several times, including an October 2022 blast in which an explosive-packed truck was detonated on the bridge, causing months of disruption.
Around 600 of the drones were intercepted on approach to the Russian capital, Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
The interceptions came hours after Ukrainian forces struck a major Russian petrochemical plant, an oil refinery and a military production site.
Kyiv says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Moscow's own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid -- attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions.
Russia says Estonian border closures will backfire
Moscow has denied being behind sabotage attacks that prompted Estonia to close its border with Russia, implying the decision would only backfire on Tallinn.
Estonia announced Sunday it was closing border checkpoints with its ex-Soviet neighbour after saying it had thwarted an attempted arson attack by Russia's GRU military intelligence on a drone factory.
"These statements have no basis whatsoever ... no evidence, nothing," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday.
"They are absolutely unfounded and we cannot take such accusations seriously," he added, referring to what he called "similar accusations" from other European countries.
Several countries across the EU have accused Russia of being behind sabotage attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine, in what many see as a rise of so-called "hybrid warfare."
Tallinn said the borders would close on December 1.
"Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls," Peskov said.
Estonia, a member of the European Union and NATO, currently has three crossing points with Russia at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula, that allow the movement of people and goods between the two countries.
Russia suspended vehicle traffic through Narva in February 2024, although pedestrians were still allowed to pass.
The crossings are among the few remaining overland links between Russia and the European Union still operating since Moscow launched its full-scale offensive on Ukraine in February 2022.
Irish diplomat steps down as envoy
David O'Sullivan, a former senior Irish civil servant at EU level, has confirmed he is stepping down as the EU's Russia sanctions envoy.
In a brief statement to RTÉ News, Mr O'Sullivan said: "I'm stepping down because I've done four years and I think it’s time for somebody new to take over."
Mr O’Sullivan was appointed by the European Commission as International Special Envoy for the Implementation of EU Sanctions in December 2022, tasked with ensuring that third countries complied with sanctions against Russia over its invasion of Ukraine.
He has spent the past four years meeting governments across the globe to press against circumvention of sanctions, with Russia frequently finding ways to evade export controls.
Before taking up the role, Mr O’Sullivan was Director-General of the Institute of International and European Affairs (IIEA) in Dublin and had served as EU ambassador to the United States.
He was the chief operating officer of the EU’s diplomatic arm, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and had been secretary general of the European Commission between 2005-2010.
Mr O’Sullivan has commented on the government’s response to the allegations surrounding Aughinish Alumina’s exports of alumina to Russia.
At an IIEA meeting in October, Mr O’Sullivan said he had "no doubt the investigative journalists got it right", adding that: "The alumina goes to smelters in Russia, who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex."
It’s understood the European Commission is seeking a replacement for Mr O’Sullivan to take up the sanctions envoy role.
Additional reporting: AFP, Reuters
